question: The European Union plans to cut free emission allocations under the Emissions Trading System (ETS) by 34 % for the period 2026-2030. This drastic reduction in emission allowances for domestic industries will have a huge negative impact on several sectors, including Spain’s ceramic industry (concentrated in the Community of Valencia), which is expecting to be hit by additional costs of over EUR 180 million.

Recently, the Commission put forward proposals designed to mitigate the adverse effects of the ETS, since the system itself proves to be incompatible with the competitiveness and productivity of Europe’s industry, as well as with maintaining and creating jobs. In light of the fact that the Commission has put forward measures to reduce the consequences of the ETS, admitting that it is not viable: 1.
What justifies maintaining and tightening measures that are known to harm EU industry and employment, and which foreign state will benefit the most?
Does the Commission intend to take specific action to mitigate the adverse effect that reducing free emission allocations by 34 % will have on the Spanish ceramic sector?
What interest groups have led the Commission to prioritise tightening the ETS, as well as to ignore the calls from Spain’s ceramic industry?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The legislation on the Emission Trading System (ETS) provides for transitional free allocation to evolve and decline in time. The reduction rates are in line with the objective of economy-wide climate neutrality by 2050 and the interim reduction targets.

The 2026-2030 benchmark update exercise, including the applied methodology, is a legal obligation enshrined in the ETS Directive1 that the Commission has no discretion to deviate from without creating uncertainty and imposing a significant delay to the process of determining and transferring the 2026 free allocation to industry.

The concerns expressed by industry have been well noted and are taken into account by the Commission. The Commission is applying all the flexibilities that are possible within the existing legal framework set by the ETS Directive.

The upcoming review of the ETS Directive will review the rules on free allocation and consider how to best support and boost investments in decarbonisation and electrification of the sectors covered by the system. Commission will also propose the introduction of an empowerment to introduce further sector-specific fallback benchmarks.
